labels.label: bdef:omega_lambda

hypotheses.note: used only for the disjointness of Omega^+ and Omega^-

findings: The sentence closing Def 4.4 (l.901-902), 'If Lambda contains at least 2 elements, then Omega^pm(Lambda), if nonempty, is regular', is false under Def 4.5 for non-closed Lambda: Lambda = {u0} x ]0,inf[ has many elements and Omega^+ = {<v|p> <= 0}, nonempty and not open (not_futureRegular_ray). For closed Lambda it holds with any number of elements (Lemma 4.8). The number of elements is not the relevant condition; closedness is.
The observations l.907-911 (convex, future/past complete, Omega^+ and Omega^- disjoint) are all true; disjointness needs Lambda nonempty (l.882).

[4.J] normalisation slip, l.782-783 and l.785-789: on {N(v) = 1, |v| = 0} one has x0^2 = sum xi^2 = 1/2, so 'necessarily x0 = 1/2' should read x0 = 1/sqrt 2, and the induced metric is the round metric of the sphere of radius 1/sqrt 2, not of the unit sphere. The Lean parametrisation (nullVec u = (1,u), u on the unit sphere) is related to Barbot's by (u,s) -> (nullVec u/sqrt 2, s/sqrt 2); nothing downstream depends on the radius, and the conformal factor a(g,v) = 1/N(L(g)v) is the same in both normalisations.
questions: l.909 'geodesically complete in the future' is read as J^+(Omega^+) subset Omega^+ and its ray form p + t v, v future causal, t >= 0; in Minkowski space these coincide.

labels.label: bdef:regular_domain
questions: Def 4.5 counts a singleton Lambda as regular (Omega^+ an open half-space), while l.1001-1003 and l.901 suggest regular domains come from Lambda 'not reduced to one point' (Bonsante's convention?). The Lean definition follows Def 4.5 literally; should a singleton be excluded?

labels.label: bprop:regular_iff_bounded

hypotheses.note: weakened for the nonemptiness half: Omega^+(Lambda) nonempty iff s bounded below, for every Lambda

findings: SIGN ERROR confirmed. The statement (l.1011-1013) says future regular iff s < C (resp. past regular iff s > C); the proof (l.1017-1031) shows Lambda subset {s > C} implies Omega^+ nonempty and Omega^+ nonempty implies s bounded below. With P^+ = {<v|p> - s < 0} (l.887-890) the correct statement is: closed Lambda is future regular iff s is bounded BELOW, past regular iff bounded ABOVE (proved). The printed form is refuted for every d >= 1 (Barbot n >= 2) by Lambda = S x [0,inf[, closed, future regular (Omega^+ = open future cone of 0) and unbounded above.

labels.label: bcor:futetpast

hypotheses.paper: Lambda closed (not printed; standing convention l.1001-1009)
hypotheses.note: needed: the compact => regular direction holds without it

findings: Corollary 4.11 needs Lambda closed, which it does not print: Lambda = {u0} x ([0,1] minus {1/2}) is future and past regular (Omega^+ = P^+(u0,0), Omega^- = P^-(u0,1)) and not compact (futureRegular_pastRegular_not_isCompact). With Lambda closed it is proved. Unmarked only because the closedness is a reading of l.1001-1009; if the author rules that the convention covers 4.11, the row is closed as it stands.
questions: Does the standing convention of l.1001-1004 ('regular convex domains ... associated to closed sets Lambda') cover Corollary 4.11? If yes, mark it.

labels.label: bprop:laoucapulse
findings: 'Expanding' is undefined, and the reading matters. g.(v,s) = ([L]v, a(g,v)s) with tau = 0; the s-component has v-derivative s * d_v a, so off s = 0 the differential is not conformal (it is the matrix [[a R, 0], [s grad a, a]]). In the metric reading (LaoucapulseMetricReading: expanding at x = some l > 1 with l*dist <= dist(f,f) near x) Prop 4.2 (l.859-865) is FALSE, and this is now proved in Lean for d = 2 (Barbot's n = 3): not_laoucapulseMetricReading_two. Counterexample: the boost Laoucapulse.boostIsom with cosh = 5/4, sinh = 3/4 in the (t, x) plane, u0 = (-3/5, 4/5) where a(g,u0) = 5/4 > 1 (so [L(g)] is expanding at u0), and the point (u0, 4) of J+ where g is not expanding: along the curve t -> (R_t u0, s(t)), R_t the rotation with tan(theta/2) = t, s(t) = 4 c(R_t u0)/c(u0), the two images have the same s-component and the image distance is at most the distance (squared: 6.25 t^2 against 36 t^2 as t -> 0). The Lean metric is the sup product of the chordal metric and |.|; the counterexample transfers (argument in SCOPE, not formalized) to Barbot's Riemannian product of the round metric and any euclidean metric on R. The statement holds for volume expansion (Jacobian a^d > 1 iff a > 1, d >= 2), which is the only reading the common-factor remark l.849-851 justifies.
questions: Which meaning of 'expanding' does Prop 4.2 intend: volume expansion, or expansion of every tangent vector? Its use in the loxodromic case (blem:loxregular, §10) should say which is needed.

kb_proposals: Past halves of statements about half-spaces of Minkowski space come cheaply from the point reflection p -> -p together with (u,s) -> (u,-s) (omegaMinus_eq_neg, Homeomorph.preimage_closure/interior); minkowski d has no dual identification with itself in the library, so C.dual does not apply here.

In Minkowski space ANY causally convex open set is globally hyperbolic on W (globallyHyperbolicOn_of_causallyConvexIn): le_W agrees with le_top on W because the straight segment of a causal pair stays in the diamond; convexity is not needed. Future- or past-complete open sets are the special case.
Inside `theorem Foo.closure`, the identifier `closure` resolves to the theorem itself: name such lemmas otherwise (FutureRegular.closure_futureRegular).

A concrete element of lorentz d (det = 1) is cheap: write the map by coordinates, conjugate by a hand-made LinearEquiv to Fin (d+1) -> R, then LinearMap.det_conj, LinearMap.det_toMatrix', Matrix.det_fin_three and one simp (Laoucapulse.boostL_mem in Flat/Penrose.lean).

To get <=_W from a causal pair whose segment lies in an open W, thicken the segment: IsCompact.exists_thickening_subset_open gives a convex open thickening inside W, Form.le_iff_of_convex applies to it, then le_mono (le_of_le_top_of_segment_subset); no curve needs to be built by hand.
